reports.question: Investigate why this mathematical calculation did not prove the reach-and-hold task feasible. Check solver status, principal violated constraints, exact values and units, time coverage, model and validity limits. Distinguish failed search from infeasibility; identify unresolved questions.

interpretations.text: The calculation was a failed numerical search, not a proof of infeasibility. SLSQP terminated with status 9, “Iteration limit reached,” after 100 iterations (the 100-iteration maximum), with success=false. The computation therefore produced neither a verified feasible witness nor an exclusion certificate; the mathematical conclusion is explicitly inconclusive. Replay consistency was nevertheless excellent: maximum prediction replay error was 1.7208456881689926e-15, and all 13 requested samples over the full 0–0.35 s horizon were checked. The operating point was not static equilibrium, and its target-position distance was 0.053749418601506754 m; this is a task-target distance, not a force or mechanical-equilibrium residual.

The principal sampled violations were extremely small but strict. The holding position-error limit was 0.01 m, while the maximum recorded value was 0.010000056805892363 m at t=0.30 s, exceeding the limit by 5.68058923632736e-08 m. The holding speed limit was 0.02 m/s, while the maximum was 0.02000489088519356 m/s at t=0.33 s, exceeding it by 4.890885193561262e-06 m/s. Additional speed violations occurred at 0.30 s, 0.31 s, and 0.35 s. Terminal error passed at 0.009657911738682468 m against the 0.01 m limit. Thus the candidate failed the sampled acceptance checks because of holding constraints, despite satisfying the terminal position constraint; the reported maximum normalized violation was only 0.0002445442596780631.

The evidence cannot determine whether the small violations reflect solver stagnation, the non-equilibrium operating point, model limitations, or genuine infeasibility. The calculation used frozen local affine dynamics with exact zero-order hold, six tendon tensions bounded from 0 to 8 N, a 0.01 s control period, and sampled rather than continuous-time constraints. It does not establish continuous-time compliance, global nonlinear feasibility or infeasibility, hardware performance, robustness, repeatability, or physical task acceptance. The full declared horizon was covered at discrete samples, but between-sample behavior remains unresolved. No diagnostic relations or independent comparison evidence identify a failure mechanism, so additional claims about cause would be hypotheses rather than conclusions.

reports.question: Investigate these two independent reach-and-hold evaluations. Give principal violations, times and numerical values. Compare the second listed result as the baseline: which quantities improved or worsened, and is the comparison valid? Separate measured facts from possible mechanisms and competing explanations. No single-factor causal attribution from confounded changes.

interpretations.text: Both evaluations were valid, complete task evaluations but failed acceptance because the sole principal violation was holding speed during the holding window at t = 0.30–0.35 s. In the first-listed result, holding speed was 0.05203049356582944 m/s against a 0.02 m/s limit, exceeding the limit by 0.03203049356582944 m/s; its normalized signed excess was 1.6015246782914723. Terminal position error was 0.0027808380549602055 m, holding position error was 0.0030310250356348953 m, force-bound violation was 0.0 N, and solver errors were 0. The second-listed result, used as baseline, likewise failed only holding speed: 0.022849089710631265 m/s against 0.02 m/s, an excess of 0.002849089710631265 m/s and normalized signed excess 0.14245448553156326. Its terminal and holding position errors were both 0.0031364418844500026 m; force-bound violation and solver errors were 0.0 N and 0, respectively. The recorded critical observations for both occurred at t = 0.35000000000000003 s. Neither result demonstrates task acceptance, despite valid evaluation and zero solver errors.

Relative to the second-listed baseline, the first-listed result improved the lower-is-better terminal position error by 0.00035560382948979707 m, from 0.0031364418844500026 m to 0.0027808380549602055 m, and improved holding position error by 0.00010541684881510728 m, from 0.0031364418844500026 m to 0.0030310250356348953 m. Force-bound violation and solver-error count were unchanged at 0.0 N and 0. The comparison is valid only as descriptive arithmetic: the supplied relation explicitly marks the results as non-comparable for causal inference because design identity, control source, and model identity are unknown, and structure and control changed. Therefore, the first result did not establish that any particular factor caused the positional improvements. The same arithmetic shows worsening in holding speed: it increased by 0.029181403855198178 m/s, from the baseline 0.022849089710631265 m/s to 0.05203049356582944 m/s, moving farther beyond the 0.02 m/s threshold. Both evaluations also had 35 deadline misses, no demonstrated real-time execution, and unavailable tension/control diagnostics; these observations do not identify a mechanism.

The evidence cannot distinguish among competing mechanisms for the speed violation or for the opposing position-versus-speed changes. Possible explanations include differences in structure, controller, model, initial state, input realization, or numerical execution, but the recorded outcomes alone do not identify any one of them. The common 0.35 s endpoint and discrete samples do not establish continuous-time compliance or behavior between samples. The first result's larger numerical wall time (3210.219000000041 s in the acceptance record; resource record 3212.3950461999048 s) versus the baseline (3316.3910000000615 s; resource record 3321.8154292001855 s) also cannot be interpreted causally as a performance change. A causal comparison would require matched design, model, control source, task, initial conditions, inputs, timing grid, and thresholds, together with the unavailable control diagnostics and relevant trajectories.

reports.question: Using the already delivered Reporter findings and saved result references, synthesize the reliable conclusions about the sealed S142 reach-and-hold failures, distinguish mathematical-search failure from physical task failure, compare competing explanations, and identify the most important unresolved questions. Do not launch any new analysis or repeat identical detailed reads.

interpretations.text: The sealed S142 evidence separates a valid physical task failure from an inconclusive mathematical search. Two complete registered executions were valid but rejected solely for holding speed: 0.0520304936 m/s versus the 0.020 m/s limit, and 0.0228490897 m/s versus the same limit. Their holding-position errors were compliant (0.0030310250 m and 0.0031364419 m, respectively, against 0.010 m), force-bound violations were 0 N, and solver-error counts were zero. Thus the observed failures are physical-task acceptance failures, specifically excessive motion during the holding window, not execution invalidity or demonstrated position failure. The evidence does not establish why the speeds were excessive. In particular, the recorded comparisons are not causally attributable because design identity, control source, model identity, and complete matched conditions are not established; unequal outcomes therefore cannot isolate structure, control, or another mechanism.

The numerical trajectory attempt does not support a claim of global infeasibility or a physical impossibility result. SLSQP reached its 100-iteration limit with success=false and status 9, so the mathematical conclusion is explicitly inconclusive and no verified witness or exclusion certificate exists. The replayed sampled affine trajectory was finite and internally reproduced to 1.72×10^-15 m, but it failed two sampled holding constraints by very small absolute amounts: position 0.0100000568 m versus 0.010 m, and maximum speed 0.0200048909 m/s versus 0.020 m/s. The terminal error passed at 0.0096579117 m versus 0.010 m. These are local, sampled-model diagnostics only; they do not demonstrate continuous-time compliance, nonlinear feasibility or infeasibility, equilibrium validity, hardware performance, or task acceptance. The 0.0537494186 m target-position distance is a distance to the target, not a mechanical-equilibrium residual, and cannot explain the failure by itself.

The central unresolved issue is whether the physical holding-speed failures arise from the selected operating point, controller behavior, model mismatch, structural limitations, timing or another mechanism. Current evidence cannot discriminate these explanations: the diagnostic relations require matched candidate, task, initial state, inputs, model and time grid, and finite sampled observations do not establish between-sample dynamics. The mathematical attempt also leaves unresolved whether a compliant trajectory exists outside the terminated local search, while the physical records lack actual tension diagnostics. Important missing evidence includes a controlled, identity-matched comparison with complete task and timing definitions, the corresponding actual inputs and initial states, and evidence linking model predictions to the registered physical trajectories. Until such evidence exists, the reliable conclusion is failure of the tested physical executions and failure of this particular numerical search attempt—not structural infeasibility, controller causation, or general task impossibility.
